Society & Human Rights
• Egypt’s press-freedom climate drew fresh scrutiny as a court adjourned the retrial of Mada Masr editor Lina Attalah, who faces “false news” charges the UN warns are part of wider assaults on journalism.
• Mass labor unrest escalated in Europe and Latin America: Spain’s first general strike in 14 years spotlighted a housing affordability crisis ahead of snap elections, while Chilean transport workers blocked highways over soaring fuel costs.
• Rights groups condemned a Belgian law enabling police to enter homes to remove rejected asylum seekers, calling it a “law of fear.”
• Medical and minority rights concerns intensified: advocates protested the detention of Gaza physician Dr. Abu Safia amid ongoing strikes, and Africa’s rights body urged Niger’s president to halt alleged abuses against Mahamid Arabs.
• Accountability and equity debates persisted, from a New Orleans attorney’s vindication in exposing clergy abuse to new evidence women are less likely to receive authorship credit in research.
Why it matters: Democratic norms, living costs, migration enforcement, and civil liberties are converging flashpoints shaping social stability and trust in institutions across multiple regions.

Climate & Environment
• At COP31, UN chief António Guterres warned the “climate crisis is outrunning us,” denouncing fossil-fuel lobbying as countries grapple with an electrification goal that requires quadrupling the pace of grid and clean power build-out.
• Climate finance pledges for developing nations have fallen more than 70%, even as delegates registered for COP31 reach record levels, underscoring a gap between ambition and resourcing.
• Air pollution surged in India, overwhelming monitors amid toxic smog, highlighting public-health stakes of delayed clean air and energy transitions.
• The UK announced a record £12bn offshore wind investment, while research flagged AI datacentres’ plans for 181GW of on-site gas power as a growing climate risk.
• Conservation headlines ranged from flood-driven water surges into New Mexico’s Navajo Reservoir to ongoing wildlife disease crises and habitat fragmentation concerns.
Why it matters: With finance, political will, and infrastructure lagging, 2020s climate decisions will lock in emissions, security risks, and health impacts for decades.

Health & Pandemic
• Kenya discharged its last Ebola patient and started a 42‑day countdown to virus-free status, while the Democratic Republic of Congo’s deadliest outbreak surpassed 11,000 cases.
• The US risks losing measles elimination status amid its worst outbreak since 1991, as vaccine hesitancy reshapes public-health challenges.
• England and Scotland ordered poultry housed again due to avian influenza risks; separately, research examined how icons can improve reading for people with aphasia.
Why it matters: Diverging outbreak trajectories and vaccine adherence determine whether health systems contain resurgent and emergent threats.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwe9kzv0g0v7o https://www.npr.org/2026/11/11/nx-s1-6037304/ebola-congo-outbreak https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/11/measles-status-rfk-jr-anti-vaccine-agenda https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/11/bird-flu-poultry-captive-birds-kept-inside-england-scotland

Armed Conflict & Security
• Coordinated bomb hoax emails disrupted hundreds of schools across Italy and also hit Scotland and Ireland, part of a spate of Europe-focused nuisance attacks.
• The UK and partners unveiled a Northern European framework to jointly develop drones and warship capabilities to deter Russia, as a US soldier was arrested in Britain on Russia spying allegations.
• El Salvador’s military coordinated with Haiti against the 400 Mawozo gang in a cross-border bid to confront spiraling gang violence; in India, a passenger train derailed in Assam, injuring several.
Why it matters: Hybrid threats, espionage cases, and cross-border security operations underscore the diffuse and evolving nature of regional security risks.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwz0k79pr8z2o https://www.ft.com/content/7bbc0a5e-b7e2-4a3f-874f-a63de94e922d?syn-25a6b1a6=1 https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/11/whats-northern-europes-new-drones-and-warships-plan-to-counter-russia https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/11/us-soldier-arrested-for-russia-spying-what-we-know https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg2xdwnwezo

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• The US House blocked—for now—an impeachment bid against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a procedural win for the administration even as partisan tensions persist.
• Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large prisoner exchange after US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, marking the biggest humanitarian release since 2022.
• Washington warned Madagascar over deepening military ties with Russia; France pressed Germany to clarify doctrine on long-range “deep precision strikes” to avoid nuclear escalation risks.
• The US skipped a key UN human rights review for a second year, worrying rights groups about accountability norms; scrutiny also grew over North Korea’s succession signaling and Indonesia’s vice president offering resignation amid political rifts.
Why it matters: Tactical diplomatic gains coexist with widening trust gaps on rights and security that will shape conflict dynamics and alliances into 2027.

Sports

Why it matters: Athlete availability, league structures, and event scheduling reflect the commercial and competitive pressures shaping global sport.

Entertainment
• Apple will shut down its Support Community forum next week, ending a long-running user troubleshooting hub; Sony will retire the PlayStation Plus PC streaming app on Dec. 10.
• Disney is bringing 60+ 3D films, including The Avengers and Black Panther, to the Disney Plus app on Meta Quest, expanding premium VR content.
• Coachella 2027 will be headlined by Dua Lipa, Tame Impala, and SZA, while documentary “NAZA” surpassed 1.5 million admissions worldwide.
• Sony canceled the live-service heist shooter Fairgames; Ableton announced Live 13 with step sequencing and new drum synth tools for early 2027.
Why it matters: Shifting platform priorities, immersive content investments, and festival lineups signal where audiences—and revenue—are headed across music, film, and gaming.

Economy & Markets
• AI enthusiasm steadied markets: CoreWeave beat estimates and lifted guidance, and Anthropic’s IPO was multiple times oversubscribed, helping US tech futures rebound despite hot inflation.
• Nvidia shares bounced as investors assessed whether scrutiny of CEO Jensen Huang could spill into operations.
• Japan’s Nissan cut petrol car output and pivoted toward EVs and hybrids in China amid a harsh price war; Volkswagen scrapped an advanced factory plan as it rethinks investment in Germany.
• ITV cut costs and trimmed Q4 content spend amid a UK ad slump as its sale of TV and streaming assets to Sky progresses under regulatory review.
• Saudi Arabia told OPEC its oil output surged 26% to a wartime high, pressuring prices; US mortgage rates fell for a fourth week, lifting purchase applications.
Why it matters: AI-fueled capital markets, auto-sector resets, and energy supply shifts are pulling asset prices in different directions as rates and inflation remain pivotal.

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• A Nature Aging study links aging-related lipid remodeling to impaired NK cell mechanics and reduced tumor surveillance, identifying ELOVL6 as a potential target.
• Researchers reported vanadyl sulfate, a common supplement, killed senescent cells and extended male mice lifespan in late-life treatment, while other work probed CSF flow stagnation in Alzheimer’s.
• Efforts to calibrate multi-compound supplements showed modest effects on vascular aging measures, underscoring the need to weigh effect sizes rigorously.
Why it matters: Pinpointing immune and clearance pathways—and testing senolytics—could yield practical interventions to extend healthy years.
Sources: https://www.nature.com/articles/s43587-026-01262-4 https://lifespan.io/a-supplement-kills-senescent-cells-and-extends-life-in-mice/ https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/11/evidence-for-cerebrospinal-fluid-flow-through-the-brain-to-stagnate-in-alzheimers-disease/ https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/11/calibrating-effects-of-a-novel-supplement-strategy-on-vascular-measures-of-aging/

Artificial Intelligence
• OpenAI introduced verified “Business Agents” and new business profiles for ChatGPT, aiming to make the chatbot a consumer discovery and support layer for brands.
• Google rolled out its Gemini 4 Carbon model publicly, touting an agent “swarm” feature; Anthropic launched Claude Meetings and an enterprise office suite to turn discussions into plans and tasks.
• New York’s AI safety law took effect, requiring major developers to register and disclose safety practices; eBay appeared to block third-party AI agents from browsing its platform.
• CoreWeave beat revenue and raised guidance, easing AI slowdown fears, while commentary highlighted risks posed by governance crises around Nvidia’s leadership.
Why it matters: The AI stack is racing from models to agents and enterprise workflows amid rising regulatory scrutiny and uneven platform cooperation.

Science & Technology
• Smart TV makers are collecting extensive user data beyond what’s needed for functionality, raising privacy questions as new devices embed ad tech and analytics by default.
• SpaceX unveiled Starlink Mini 2 with a swappable battery and moved Starship’s Super Heavy booster to the pad for tests ahead of a first double-catch attempt on Nov. 13.
• Microsoft released Automatic Super Resolution upscaling (a DLSS rival) across the Xbox Ally X family and select Copilot+ PCs; Seagate revived hybrid SSD-HDD drives.
• A coding agent platform leak exposed thousands of apps’ confidential data, underscoring persistent security lapses in developer tools and AI-assisted pipelines.
• NASA marked Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth and highlighted studies on using gravitational waves to reveal exoplanets, while researchers probed tougher-than-expected quantum error correction.
Why it matters: Consumer tech privacy, launch cadence, AI-accelerated tools, and frontier science advances are reshaping daily life and strategic capabilities.

Art & Culture
• A science fiction novel won the Booker Prize for the first time, signaling a potential shift in the literary establishment’s embrace of genre fiction.
• Gaza-focused documentary “NAZA” passed 1.5 million cinema admissions, ranking among the year’s most-watched documentaries.
• New festival and awards highlights included FilmLight Colour Awards winners and premieres at Tallinn exploring self-discovery, love, and war.
Why it matters: Cultural gatekeeping is evolving as audiences and juries reward stories that bridge genre, politics, and personal narratives.

Other

Society & Human Rights.text: PM, in response to Ed Davey at PMQs, says measures could help address ‘poisonous politics’Here are some more comments on the report for the Casey commission released today looking at how social care is run in England. (See 9.56am.)This is from Natasha Curry, deputy director of research at the Nuffield Trust and one of the report’s authors.Compared to the other countries we looked at, the governance of England’s social care system is confused and complex. Overlapping and unclear roles leave dangerous uncertainty around who is responsible for important decisions, contributing to the inertia around reform England has struggled with for decades. The serious consequences of this were laid bare during the Covid pandemic.The system for governing adult social care in England has evolved haphazardly and with little clear planning. That has been exacerbated by successive governments ducking politically unpalatable decisions for decades. That has scattered responsibility for the sector across and outside government in a way that few would design from scratch.This report makes for sober reading of how adult social care and those who rely on it have been systematically failed. Climate & Environment.text: As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hardIt began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1).By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. Climate & Environment.title: Why are Britain's streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them | George Monbiot
Climate & Environment.text: The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardiceThis is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks. It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it isn’t ready, so the government must delay its plans.This is what triggered the Dutch nitrate crisis, and the UK’s repeated “emergency” exemptions from the ban on a devastating class of pesticides. Sports.title: Formula 1 Confirms the 2026 Season Will End in Qatar and Abu Dhabi
Sports.text: SummaryFormula One pushes ahead with Qatar and Abu Dhabi for the 2026 season finaleImola officially stood down as a back-up venue despite regional conflict concernsFIA president commits to delivering two outstanding Grands Prix to close the yearFormula 1 is locking in its scheduled Middle East races to close out the 2026 season, officially standing down its back-up contingency plans. The Italian circuit of Imola, located just 20 miles from Bologna, had been actively lined up to replace Abu Dhabi as the final host venue amid major concerns over the ongoing conflict in the region. The Qatar race is slated to take place on November 29, leading directly into the Abu Dhabi round that will decisively wrap up the championship calendar on December 6.The decision to proceed with the Middle East finale follows severe disruptions earlier in the year, which forced organizers to restructure the calendar. As the outbreak of war triggered widespread alarm earlier in the year, Formula One canceled its scheduled April rounds in both Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. Organizers relocated the canceled Bahrain event to Malaysia, where it took place in September 2026. Management's renewed confidence in finishing the season as originally planned stems directly from the geopolitical situation having somewhat stabilized in recent months, though trackside safety remains heavily scrutinized by all involved parties.The delicate balance of committing to the region while maintaining a hard line on security was the central focus of a high-level meeting between key stakeholders that took place on November 10. During this session, Formula One teams sought out specific details and assurances regarding contingency plans in the event that an escalation occurs during the actual race weeks. Despite the elevated stakes, no Formula One teams have expressed an unwillingness to travel to the Middle East for the final two races. Instead, the teams have consistently expressed confidence in the sport and the governing body, the FIA, trusting leadership to make the right decision over exactly where to end the season safely.Even with the grid fully on board to travel, safety remains the undisputed leading concern. Formula One chiefs remain completely prepared to pull the events should a regional escalation happen in the coming weeks. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem took to Instagram on Tuesday to publicly back the final stretch. Ben Sulayem stated that the organization is "fully prepared and committed to delivering two outstanding Grands Prix weekends." The president added that leadership is working closely with partners to ensure everything is securely in place for drivers, teams and fans, betting that the stabilized climate will hold to crown a champion.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Rockstar Confirms GTA VI Will Run at 30 FPS on Current-Gen Consoles Ahead of Its November 19 Launch
Entertainment.text: SummaryRockstar Games opens console pre-loads and drops a new trailer ahead of the highly anticipated November 19 launchThe title targets 30 fps while pushing hardware limits to render the dense, visually unmatched world of LeonidaA landmark 10-year partnership brings day-one Xbox Cloud Gaming support and signals a major ecosystem expansionRockstar Games officially released a new trailer and opened servers to make Grand Theft Auto 6 available for pre-load on the Xbox Series X/S and PlayStation 5. The title is scheduled to go live on November 19. Both Xbox and PlayStation announced that the upcoming open-world title is officially the most pre-ordered game ever on their respective digital storefronts.Rockstar announced that Grand Theft Auto 6 targets a baseline performance of 30 frames per second. The studio stated that pushing current-generation platforms to their absolute limits maintains the density and visual fidelity of its setting, Leonida. Official blog posts from Rockstar made no mention of potential 40 fps or 60 fps support for the PlayStation 5 Pro. However, the upgraded hardware still offers exclusive graphical advantages. On the PlayStation 5 Pro, the title supports Sony's PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution upscaling technology. The PlayStation 5 Pro stands as the only console capable of running the game with advanced ray-traced shadows.Beyond graphical horsepower, Rockstar stated that the game features improved load times on Sony's console. The PlayStation 5 version includes integrated high-fidelity haptic feedback for DualSense controllers. To complement tactile upgrades, the experience includes spatial audio designed to utilize Tempest 3D Audio on PlayStation 5.While Sony secures exclusive hardware features, Microsoft offers streaming capabilities. Grand Theft Auto 6 includes baseline remote play support for PlayStation and Xbox, while also launching on Xbox Cloud Gaming directly on consoles including the previous-generation Xbox One. Rockstar noted that cloud streaming graphics are limited to Xbox Series S settings. This cloud access allows players on older hardware to join the release at launch without upgrading their consoles.Xbox CEO Asha Sharma posted on X that the launch marks the first step in a new 10-year strategic partnership with Rockstar parent company Take-Two. As a result of this partnership, Xbox Cloud Gaming will add support for legacy titles such as Grand Theft Auto 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 in the coming months. Securing the blockbuster for day-one streaming signals a major expansion for Microsoft's cloud ecosystem.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Nicolas Cage Revealed He Felt Relieved Over 'Spider-Noir' Cancelation at Prime Video
Entertainment.text: SummaryNicolas Cage revealed he felt relieved when Prime Video canceled 'Spider-Noir' after a single seasonThe actor stated that one season of portraying the idiosyncratic Ben Reilly was perfect to avoid wearing out his welcomeDespite pulling 2.6 billion viewing minutes and five Emmy wins the series ended following tensions surrounding an AI waiverHollywood actor Nicolas Cage has revealed he felt relieved following Prime Video's decision to cancel Spider-Noir after only one season. Speaking in an interview with IGN, the National Treasure star praised the solitary run of the live-action comic adaptation as "perfect" and emphasized that he had no interest in wearing out his welcome by continuously reprising the idiosyncratic character of private investigator Ben Reilly.“It’s a perfect season. You never wanna get stuck repeating a character and wear out your welcome,” Cage explained. “Ben Riley is so idiosyncratic. I was doing something that was pretty high-risk, tightrope stuff — if you do that for Season 2, Season 3, you could really wear out your welcome. So when they didn’t pick it up, I was like, ‘Whew, thank you!’ Because now I’m doing True Detective, and that’s only one season. It’s better that way, you know? I didn’t wanna keep repeating it. I don’t like repeating myself.”Despite drawing 2.6 billion viewing minutes within its opening six weeks and earning five Emmy wins across 11 nominations, the series came to an abrupt close. The cancellation also followed friction surrounding artificial intelligence, with Cage revealing at New York Comic Con that he refused to sign an AI waiver for the production. Looking forward, Cage is slated to star alongside Antonio Banderas in the upcoming fifth season of HBO's True Detective and will appear in the John Madden biographical film Madden.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Jordan 4 Retro TD “Bred” Takes MJ’s ‘89 Classic From Hardwood to Turf
Entertainment.text: Name: Jordan 4 Retro TD "Bred"Colorway: Black/Cement Grey/White/Fire RedSKU: HQ0207-001MSRP: $205 USDRelease Date: November 27Where to Buy: SNKRSThe Jordan 4 Retro TD “Bred” moves Michael Jordan’s 1989 game shoe onto the football field, translating one of the most celebrated sneakers in the Jumpman catalog into a fully functional cleat. Dressed in Black, Cement Grey, White and Fire Red, the pair revives one of the AJ4’s first colorways while swapping its basketball outsole for a stud plate made for the gridiron.Few colorways carry the weight of the “Bred” 4. The black-and-red scheme was among the looks that launched the silhouette in 1989, and it has since become one of the most coveted versions of the shoe. It also has a place in playoff history, as Jordan wore the pair when he hit “The Shot” over Craig Ehlo to eliminate the Cleveland Cavaliers that same year. Bringing that colorway to football gives the cleat instant recognition before it ever touches the field.Up top, the cleat stays remarkably faithful to the original. The upper blends genuine and synthetic leather for structure and durability, with breathable textile zones working alongside the shoe’s classic detailing. A high collar and traditional lacing complete the silhouette, so from the ankle up the TD reads unmistakably as a 4, a design originally penned by Tinker Hatfield.The real transformation happens below the midsole. Jordan Brand pairs a foam midsole with Air Zoom cushioning, which is designed to deliver a springy, responsive feel each time the foot leaves the ground. Beneath it, a plate of wide molded studs bites into both turf and natural grass, giving players the grip needed for sharp lateral changes of direction and sudden bursts downfield.What results is a cleat that serves two audiences at once. Players get a performance tool built around traction and responsiveness, while collectors get one of the AJ4’s most storied colorways reworked for an entirely new arena, a reminder of how far the Jumpman legacy now extends beyond the hardwood.Set your reminders and get ahead of what’s dropping next on Hypebeast Drops.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Altra Rewrites Its Running DNA for the City With the Ease
Entertainment.text: Name: Altra EaseColorway: Black, White, GreySKU: TBCMSRP: $130 USDRelease Date: November 11Where to Buy: AltraAltra is stepping beyond running with the Ease, a brand-new sneaker silhouette that the brand calls its first lifestyle shoe after 15 years of making foot-shaped footwear for runners. Instead of designing for one setting, Altra’s design team built the Ease around the commute: the walk to the station, the bike ride across town, the coffee stop on the way to the office, the trip from the gym to dinner. The idea is that city life rarely stops; it just changes speed. “So instead of designing for a destination, we designed Ease around that constant state of transition. It’s footwear designed for the journey itself,” the team explained in an exclusive statement.The design centers on a translucent TPU exoskeleton that wraps around the shoe and gradually fades into a soft, collapsible mesh upper, leaving the supportive structure visible. From the side, the effect looks almost anatomical, like a see-through view of the foot inside. The cage holds the foot securely and carries Altra’s DNA into the vamp, where five lines run across the toe area as a nod to the natural toe splay at the heart of the brand.The rest of the shoe is built for easy, all-day wear: a plush collar with the soft give of a wetsuit, a design that’s simple to slip on, and the lowest stack height Altra has offered. Underfoot, the team kept things minimal, with refined lug geometry and clean detailing on a rubber outsole tuned for grip on city pavement. The Ease comes in three colorways: Black, White and Grey.To test the shoe in a real setting, Altra gave early pairs to Brooklyn photographer Dev Moore, who wore them across Lower Manhattan on foot and by bike for the lifestyle campaign. For Moore, the appeal is how easily the shoe fits into a full day of movement without looking out of place. “These have that balance: a sporty look that’s easy to style, with the added comfort to keep me in motion,” he said.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Measure of glymphatic drainage decline with age, and are particularly negatively impacted in patients with Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative conditions. Science & Technology.title: Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93
Science & Technology.text: Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 AugustAtal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.  Bishnu Saroop AtalNokia Bell LabsHe also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 AugustPalmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 AugustRichter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 JulyGiordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 MayWilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 MarchAmey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.
